Empirical Research Plan: Local Causal Effects at Program Cutoffs  

====================================================================  
1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
Strategy: Sharp (or, where take-up is imperfect, fuzzy) Regression-Discontinuity Design (RDD).

Justification:  
• The assignment rule is mechanical and discontinuous at a known threshold (age, score, income).  
• Economic theory suggests individuals very close to the cutoff are comparable except for treatment status, so the RD estimand identifies the local average treatment effect (LATE).  
• DID, IV, or event studies are unnecessary because cross-sectional contrasts on either side of the cutoff can be exploited directly.

====================================================================  
2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
Running variable (X): Value that determines eligibility (e.g., exact age in days, test score, annual income).  
Cutoff (c): Institutional threshold (e.g., age = 65, score = 50, income = \$25,000).  

Treatment variable (T): Indicator equal to 1 if X ≥ c, 0 otherwise.  
Control group: Observations with X < c, but within a pre-specified bandwidth |X – c| ≤ h.  
Event date / timing: Not required in a cross-sectional sharp RD. (If using panels, define relative time τ = t – policy implementation year, keep only τ = 0.)  

If compliance <100 % (e.g., some 64.9-year-olds pre-enroll), estimate fuzzy RD using T as instrument for actual receipt.

====================================================================  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes in X at c.  
  • Plausible because individuals cannot instantly change fundamental traits (health, earnings, etc.) exactly at the threshold.  

A2. No precise manipulation of X around c.  
  • Plausible for age-based rules; less so for income or test scores (teachers may coach). Will test via McCrary density test.  

A3. Covariates evolve smoothly in X at c.  
  • Administrative and survey data record demographics that should not jump at the threshold; test by running RD on predetermined variables.  

A4. Local stable treatment effect.  
  • Requires no other policy or macro shock changes exactly at c. Supported by institutional knowledge (e.g., only Medicare kicks in on 65th birthday).  

A5. Correct bandwidth and functional form chosen.  
  • Addressed through data-driven MSE-optimal bandwidth and robustness checks with alternative kernels / polynomials.

====================================================================  
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Manipulation / sorting at the threshold (especially with income or test scores).  
  • Test density (McCrary) and histograms.  
  • If evidence of sorting, switch to local randomization design or use donut RD (omit a narrow window around c).  

T2. Other policies kick in at the same cutoff.  
  • Collect a policy calendar; include controls or analyse a narrower window to isolate the target program.  
  • If unavoidable, interpret estimate as combined effect or look for alternative cutoffs without co-inciding policies.  

T3. Functional-form misspecification / bandwidth choice.  
  • Use rdrobust’s local polynomial (bias-corrected) estimator with MSE-optimal h.  
  • Report results across ±25 %, ±50 % of optimal h, and both linear and quadratic specifications.

====================================================================  
5. R Code Outline  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast read
library(rdrobust)     # RD estimation
library(ggplot2)
library(fixest)       # for covariate continuity checks

# 1. Load Data ------------------------------------------------------
# Assume one file per context; example: age_cutoff.csv
dt <- fread("age_cutoff.csv")   # id, age_days, treated, outcome, covariates...

# 2. Variable Construction -----------------------------------------
cutoff <- 65 * 365.25           # age 65 in days
dt[, running := age_days - cutoff]          # center at cutoff
dt[, treat := as.integer(running >= 0)]     # sharp treatment

# 3. Main RD --------------------------------------------------------
# rdrobust automatically chooses bandwidth; include covariates if desired
rd_main <- rdrobust(y = dt$outcome,
                    x = dt$running,
                    covs = dt[, .(male, race_white, pre_income)],
                    fuzzy = NULL)            # set fuzzy=dt$actual_takeup for Fuzzy RD
summary(rd_main)

# 4. Graphical Check ----------------------------------------------
ggplot(dt[abs(running)<=365], aes(running, outcome)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2) +
  labs(x = "Days from cutoff", y = "Outcome")

# 5. Density (McCrary) Test ---------------------------------------
rdmc <- rddensity(dt$running)
summary(rdmc)
plot(rdmc)

# 6. Covariate Continuity (Placebo RD) -----------------------------
covars <- c("male", "race_white", "pre_income")
lapply(covars, function(v){
  feols(get(v) ~ treat + poly(running,2), data = dt[abs(running)<=2*rd_main$h])
})

# 7. Robustness: Alternative bandwidth -----------------------------
for(h in c(0.5, 1, 1.5)*rd_main$h){
  print(rdrobust(dt$outcome, dt$running, h = h)$coef)
}

# 8. Placebo Cutoffs ----------------------------------------------
placebo_pts <- seq(-3*365, 3*365, by = 365)  # yearly fake cutoffs
placebo_res <- sapply(placebo_pts, function(p){
  rdrobust(dt$outcome, dt$running - p)$coef[1]
})
```

====================================================================  
6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
Economic intuition (example: Medicare at 65).  
• Direction: Positive jump in healthcare utilization and possibly health outcomes.  
• Magnitude: Back-of-the-envelope—previous literature finds ~20 % increase in doctor visits, ~4 pp reduction in out-of-pocket spending. I expect a 15–25 % increase in utilization outcomes local to 65.

====================================================================  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Sharp RD)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: No precise manipulation of running variable ………………… 1  
C2: Continuity of baseline covariates at cutoff …………………… 1  
C3: Correct bandwidth & polynomial choice / robustness ………… 1  
C4: No other discontinuous policies at cutoff …………………… 0 (possible co-policies)  
C5: Sufficient density of observations on both sides …………… 1  

Total = 4 / 5.
